theme: O God, you have rejected us
readingInstruction: Read Psalm 60. David prays after a military setback and ends with confidence in God. Notice the movement from complaint to promise to prayer.
settingTheScene: The title of Psalm 60 places it in a time when David fought Aram and Edom, and Joab struck down 12,000 Edomites in the Valley of Salt (see 2 Samuel 8). It reflects an initial defeat before the victory. It follows Psalm 44 as a second corporate lament, but ends with more resolve. It is a prayer of a king and nation that have been shaken.
observation: “O God, you have rejected us, broken our defenses; you have been angry; oh, restore us” (v. 1).
“You have made the land to quake; you have torn it open; repair its breaches, for it totters” (v. 2).
“You have made your people see hard things; you have given us wine to drink that made us stagger” (v. 3).
“You have set up a banner for those who fear you, that they may flee to it from the bow” (v. 4).
“That your beloved ones may be delivered, give salvation by your right hand and answer us!” (v. 5).
“God has spoken in his holiness: With exultation I will divide up Shechem” (v. 6).
“Oh grant us help against the foe, for vain is the salvation of man!” (v. 11).
“With God we shall do valiantly; it is he who will tread down our foes” (v. 12).
interpretation:
The psalm opens with the same bewildering confession as Psalm 44: God has rejected us. But here, the language is of an earthquake. The land has cracked open. The structure of national life is shaking. The psalmist does not blame bad luck or strategy. He sees God’s hand in it. This may seem harsh, but it is also a comfort: if God broke it, God can repair it. “Repair its breaches, for it totters.” The one who allowed the crack is the only one who can mend it.

The image of the wine that makes people stagger is strong. God has made his people drink a cup of reeling. They have “seen hard things.” The Bible does not shy away from the fact that God’s people sometimes go through suffering that disorients them.

Yet verse 4 offers a turn: “You have set up a banner for those who fear you.” A banner is a rallying point in battle. God provides a place to gather. In the midst of defeat, there is a standard to flee to. For those who fear him, he is both the one who shakes and the one who shelters.

Then, in verses 6 to 8, God speaks. His voice cuts through the confusion. He claims Shechem, Succoth, Gilead, Manasseh, Ephraim, and Judah as his. Moab, Edom, and Philistia are described as his washbasin, his sandal, and his subjects. Everything belongs to him. The promise of God’s word is the foundation of the king’s confidence.

The final prayer is one of the best in the Bible for a time of need: “Oh grant us help against the foe, for vain is the salvation of man!” Human help is empty. “With God we shall do valiantly.” The psalm ends in confidence, not because circumstances changed, but because the speaker has remembered who God is.
connection: Paul says, “If God is for us, who can be against us?” (Romans 8:31). Jesus is the banner raised for the nations (Isaiah 11:10; John 12:32). 2 Corinthians 12:9-10 shows strength made perfect in weakness. Psalm 108:6-13 repeats this psalm’s final section. 1 Corinthians 15:57: “Thanks be to God, who gives us the victory through our Lord Jesus Christ.”
application:
If something in your life feels like an earthquake, ask God to repair the breach.

Look for the “banner” God has set up for you, whether it is his word, his church, or his promise.

Pray verse 12 today: “With God we shall do valiantly.”
prayerPrompts: Ask God to repair what has been shaken in your life.
Admit that human help is vain, and ask for his.
Thank him that with him we shall do valiantly.
